title: GeoJSON Minifier: Same Data, Fewer Bytes
description: Minify GeoJSON locally in the browser with the GeoJSON Minifier — whitespace removed, data structure and values untouched. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, a 1,521-byte pretty-printed collection minifies to 669 bytes — 56.0% smaller — while every coordinate, property and feature survives byte-for-byte in value.
quick_answer: The GeoJSON Minifier minifies GeoJSON locally in your browser, stripping whitespace to shrink the text while keeping the same data structure. Paste the pretty file and download the compact one: identical geography, fewer bytes — the form files should travel in, produced without your data leaving the machine.

popular_table.note: Minified GeoJSON is still GeoJSON — RFC 7946 never required beauty. Any parser that accepts the pretty file accepts the minified one; if yours does not, the parser is the bug.

faq: What is the smallest a GeoJSON file can get?

As small as its data allows: minifying removes all whitespace, and what remains is coordinate digits and property text. Beyond this floor, only rounding decimals, dropping vertices or switching to a binary format shrinks further — different operations with real trade-offs, signposted in this page's other answers.
Will my app still parse it?
Yes — minification changes whitespace only, and JSON parsers are blind to whitespace. The minified file is the same document.
Pretty files commonly shed 30–60%, all of it air. The size calculator measures your file’s exact figure before you commit.
The Formatter re-expands minified GeoJSON losslessly — the two tools are a reversible pair, which is the definition of a safe optimisation.
Preserved — minifying removes whitespace between tokens; it does not reshuffle the document.
Values are identical; their text may normalise (40.0 → 40) through parse-and-print, as with the formatter. The geography does not move.
Should I store minified or pretty?
Store the one your humans edit (pretty), ship the one machines read (minified) — generated at build time, ideally, so the pair never drifts.
